blocks.text: Quick verdict

Infatica is the better default for location-precise scraping: it is cheaper at 10 GB ($40 against $52.50), includes ZIP targeting on every plan, and its $4 seven-day trial is an easy way to test. Compliance-minded buyers will also like its clear sourcing policy. IPRoyal is the better choice for irregular workloads and account management, because its traffic never expires and its sticky sessions run up to seven days. If you are unsure, trial Infatica first, then compare it with a 1 GB IPRoyal purchase on your real targets.

IPRoyal and Infatica are both mid-market residential providers with pools in the 30-40 million range, so neither wins on sheer size. What separates them is how they bill and what they emphasise. IPRoyal sells non-expiring traffic and very long sticky sessions; Infatica sells monthly subscriptions with ZIP-level targeting on every plan, a cheap seven-day trial and a strong ethical-sourcing story backed by ISO certifications. This comparison looks at which approach fits which kind of buyer.

blocks.text: IPRoyal in 2026: what you get

IPRoyal built its reputation on flexible, non-expiring residential bandwidth and straightforward pricing. The pool is smaller than the enterprise networks at 32M+ advertised IPs, but it covers 195 countries, supports SOCKS5, and offers some of the longest sticky sessions available (up to seven days). Its headline $1.75/GB rate only applies at 10 TB; most buyers will pay between $5 and $7 per GB on small orders.

Strengths: Residential traffic that does not expire; Sticky sessions up to 7 days; Can start with a single gigabyte; Several proxy types plus Web Unblocker in one account. Weak spots: Smaller pool than the enterprise networks; Headline $1.75/GB rate needs a 10 TB purchase; Mid-volume prices are not published.
Infatica in 2026: what you get

Infatica pitches itself on ethical sourcing and features available to every customer. All residential plans include country, city and ZIP targeting, IP whitelisting and selectable rotation times, and a 7-day $4 trial lowers the risk of testing. Independent reviewers have found its proxies fast and its pool modest but respectable. Its niche extra is a premium IPv6 residential pool, rare in this market, at about 1.5x the normal per-GB price.

Strengths: ZIP targeting included on every plan; Clear sourcing policy and ISO certifications; Cheap 7-day trial; Rare IPv6 residential pool. Weak spots: Mid-range pool size; Per-GB price stays above $3.50 until large volumes; Subscription traffic does not roll over.
Pricing: IPRoyal vs Infatica

IPRoyal's residential subscription costs $7 for 1 GB, $11.90 for 2 GB and $52.50 for 10 GB ($5.25/GB); pay-as-you-go is 5% more ($7.35 for 1 GB). The advertised $1.75/GB rate applies only at 10 TB. Prices for custom volumes such as 25, 100 or 500 GB are calculated in the dashboard.

Infatica charges $4/GB pay-as-you-go for residential traffic. Subscriptions cost $3.84/GB at 25 GB, $3.60/GB at 100 GB, and fall to about $2.70/GB at 500 GB and $2.60/GB at 1 TB. Premium IPv6 residential runs at roughly 1.5x those rates, starting at $6/GB.

Buying 10 GB, you would pay about $40 with Infatica and $52.50 with IPRoyal: a 24% saving in Infatica's favour. At 100 GB, a like-for-like total is harder to state because IPRoyal does not publish an exact price for that volume; Infatica comes to about $360. The sticker price is only half of it. IPRoyal's unused traffic carries forward, while Infatica's does not (subscription traffic resets monthly), so if your usage swings from month to month IPRoyal can work out cheaper than the per-GB numbers suggest.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

On paper the two networks are similar in size: IPRoyal advertises 32M+ residential IPs and Infatica advertises 35M-40M. Advertised pool sizes are marketing figures counted over long periods; the number of IPs actually reachable in a given country at a given moment is far smaller for every provider, so treat these as a rough guide to depth rather than a guarantee. For coverage, IPRoyal lists 195 countries and Infatica lists 195. On targeting, IPRoyal offers country, state and city (ISP selection needs verification), while Infatica offers country, state, city and ZIP.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, IPRoyal offers rotating or sticky sessions from 1 second up to 7 days, and Infatica offers per-request rotation or selectable rotation times. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With IPRoyal: solid success rates and non-expiring traffic for bursty crawls. With Infatica: fast proxies that did well on popular targets in independent tests. Run the same small test on both before committing.
SERP and rank tracking: Infatica. Infatica has the edge here. Why: ZIP targeting helps local search results. How IPRoyal compares: it works, but it has no dedicated SERP product.

Social media and multi-account management: IPRoyal. IPRoyal has the edge here. Why: 7-day sticky sessions keep one IP on one account. How Infatica compares: rotation controls are good but very long sticky sessions are not a headline feature.

E-commerce price and stock monitoring: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With IPRoyal: city targeting with pay-only-for-what-you-use traffic. With Infatica: ZIP-level targeting for local prices. Run the same small test on both before committing.

Ad verification and geo-testing: Infatica wins. The deciding factor for Infatica: precise geo targeting and clean sourcing. The limitation on the IPRoyal side: decent coverage but no ASN or carrier targeting on standard accounts.

Tight budgets: IPRoyal wins. The deciding factor for IPRoyal: small entry purchases and traffic that never expires. The limitation on the Infatica side: mid-range pricing until you reach large volumes.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. IPRoyal: No general free trial; Enterprise trial for verified companies. Infatica: 7-day trial for $4 (residential) or $8 (mobile). Verification and payment rules differ too. IPRoyal: Optional ID verification; required for ISP-level targeting and PayPal. Infatica: Standard verification; states it does not resell IPs. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test IPRoyal and Infatica before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle IPRoyal vs Infatica faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (IPRoyal: no general free trial; Enterprise trial for verified companies; Infatica: 7-day trial for $4 (residential) or $8 (mobile)).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, IPRoyal comes out ahead in 2, Infatica in 2, and 2 are ties. With no overall winner, decide on the factor that matters most to you: IPRoyal is strongest for irregular or seasonal projects, while Infatica is strongest for compliance-conscious buyers. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
